prompt: Select the city that hosts the International Atomic Energy Agency headquarters.

prompt: Select the city where delegates drafted the U.S. Constitution in 1787.

prompt: Select the upstate New York town that hosted the 1848 Women's Rights Convention.

prompt: Match each congressional committee role to a standing committee or conference committee.
explanation: Standing committees are permanent policy panels within one chamber; conference committees resolve House-Senate bill differences.
fun_fact: Both chambers must pass the exact same text of a conference report before sending it to the President.

trap_notes.default: Standing committees are permanent single-chamber panels; conference committees temporarily reconcile bills.

items.text: Extends debate to block a Senate vote
Used by the Senate minority to stall
Requires 60 senators to end debate
Moves a stalled bill toward final vote

prompt: Sort each Senate floor procedure into filibuster or cloture.
explanation: A filibuster prolongs debate to delay a vote; cloture is the 60-vote motion that ends debate.
fun_fact: The House of Representatives has strict time limits on debate and does not allow filibusters.

trap_notes.default: A filibuster delays a Senate vote through debate; cloture cuts off debate with 60 votes.

items.text: Reallocates 435 House seats after census
Shifts seats among states by population
Draws district lines for partisan gain
Uses packing and cracking strategies

prompt: Classify each redistricting concept under reapportionment or gerrymandering.
explanation: Reapportionment redistributes House seats among states every 10 years; gerrymandering manipulates district lines for advantage.
fun_fact: The term gerrymander was coined in 1812 after a salamander-shaped Massachusetts district under Governor Elbridge Gerry.

trap_notes.default: Reapportionment assigns House seat counts to states; gerrymandering draws biased district maps.

items.text: Serving on a jury when summoned
Paying federal and state income taxes
Voting in local and national elections
Volunteering in community organizations

prompt: Sort each citizen action into a mandatory legal duty or a voluntary civic responsibility.
explanation: Legal duties like jury service and taxes are required by law; civic responsibilities like voting and volunteering are voluntary.
fun_fact: Unlike the U.S., countries such as Australia and Belgium make voting a legal duty with fines.

trap_notes.default: Jury service and paying taxes are required by law; voting and volunteering are voluntary civic duties.

items.text: Grants citizenship by place of birth
Enshrined in the 14th Amendment
Grants citizenship through parents
Covers children born abroad to citizens

prompt: Match each birthright citizenship rule to jus soli or jus sanguinis.
explanation: Jus soli confers citizenship by birth on national soil; jus sanguinis confers citizenship by parentage.
fun_fact: United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898) affirmed that the 14th Amendment protects jus soli citizenship.

trap_notes.default: Jus soli ('right of soil') depends on birthplace; jus sanguinis ('right of blood') depends on parents.

items.text: Decides if probable cause supports charges
Issues a formal criminal indictment
Hears evidence during a public trial
Delivers a verdict of guilty or not

prompt: Sort each courtroom role into a grand jury or a petit (trial) jury.
explanation: Grand juries review evidence privately to issue indictments; petit juries hear trials and reach verdicts.
fun_fact: The Fifth Amendment guarantees federal grand jury indictment for capital or infamous crimes.

trap_notes.default: Grand juries decide whether to indict; petit juries hear the trial and issue a verdict.

items.text: Focuses on a narrow set of policy issues
Lobbies lawmakers without running nominees
Nominates candidates to run on ballots
Builds broad coalitions to win office

prompt: Classify each political organization trait as an interest group or a political party.
explanation: Interest groups influence policy from outside the ballot; political parties nominate candidates to win governing control.
fun_fact: Interest groups often form PACs to donate to candidates across parties who support their specific issue.

trap_notes.default: Interest groups lobby on specific issues; political parties nominate candidates to win elections.

items.text: Monarch's power is limited by a charter
Elected parliament passes national laws
Hereditary ruler holds supreme authority
No binding legislature checks the crown

prompt: Sort each governing feature into a constitutional monarchy or an absolute monarchy.
explanation: Constitutional monarchs serve mostly ceremonial roles under elected parliaments; absolute monarchs hold unchecked governing power.
fun_fact: Japan, Sweden, and the United Kingdom are modern constitutional monarchies with elected parliaments.

trap_notes.default: Constitutional monarchs are bound by law and parliament; absolute monarchs rule without legislative checks.
